title: U Tube Manometer: 5 Simple Steps for Accurate Readings
text:
Pressure

 U Tube Manometer: 5 Simple Steps for Accurate Readings

 A glass tube bent into a U and half filled with liquid is still one of the most trusted pressure instruments in any calibration room. It needs no power and no calibration chain beyond a ruler, the liquid density and gravity.

 
 ΔP = ρ g h 
 Inclined and Well Type 
 Manometer Fluids 
 Meniscus Reading 
 




 Before transmitters and digital gauges, every low pressure was read on a column of liquid. The U tube manometer still sets the reference for draft, filter and duct pressures because its physics is simple and traceable.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a U tube manometer works, how to apply the ΔP = ρ g h formula, which fluids and designs to choose and how to read the meniscus correctly.


 
 
 
 What Is a U Tube Manometer?


 A U tube manometer is a transparent tube bent into a U shape and partly filled with a liquid, where the difference in liquid level between the two legs shows the pressure difference applied across them. It is the simplest member of the instrument family covered in basics of pressure measurement .


 When both legs are open to air, the liquid stands at the same height on each side. Apply a higher pressure to one leg and the liquid is pushed down there and up in the other leg until the weight of the raised column balances the extra pressure, as Pascal law predicts.


 
 
 Image credit: Calright Instruments . Diagram courtesy of Calright Instruments, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 Because the reading depends only on height, liquid density and gravity, the instrument is called a primary standard. Nothing inside can drift the way a spring or a strain gauge drifts.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Manometer Formula and Pressure Balance


 Take a horizontal reference at the lower liquid surface. The pressure there is the same in both legs, so the applied pressure difference equals the weight of the extra column h of manometer liquid, minus the weight of the fluid sitting above it on the other side.


 
 ΔP = (ρm minus ρf) × g × h 
 Inclined tube: h = L × sin θ 
ρm = manometer liquid density, ρf = density of the fluid above it, g = 9.81 m/s²

Example, water manometer measuring air pressure:
ρm = 1000 kg/m³, ρf = 1.2 kg/m³, h = 250 mm, vertical tube
ΔP = (1000 minus 1.2) × 9.81 × 0.25
ΔP = 998.8 × 9.81 × 0.25
 ΔP = 2449.56 Pa = 2.450 kPa = 24.50 mbar 



 For gas service the term ρf is tiny and is often ignored. For liquid over the manometer fluid, such as water over mercury, it must be included or the error becomes large, a point that also matters in hydrostatic level measurement .


 Do You Know?
 A pressure of 1 inch of water column is only about 249 pascals, roughly a quarter of one percent of atmospheric pressure. Yet a good inclined manometer resolves a small fraction of that.

 Quick Tip
 Write down which leg was connected to the higher pressure before you read. A reversed connection on a differential job is one of the most common field mistakes with liquid columns.



 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Types of Liquid Column Manometers


 
 Simple U Tube
 Two equal vertical legs, read the difference between both levels.
 Best for: teaching, gas and draft checks
 Basic 

 Well Type
 One leg replaced by a large reservoir, so only one column is read.
 Best for: single reading, panel use
 Single read 

 Inclined Tube
 The reading leg is tilted at a small angle to stretch the scale.
 Best for: very low pressures, HVAC and filters
 Sensitive 

 Differential Manometer
 Both legs connected to process points.
 Best for: orifice and filter differential
 DP 




 In a well type design the reservoir area is much larger than the tube area, so the reservoir level hardly moves. Manufacturers compensate the scale for that small movement, which is why a well type scale is not graduated in true millimetres.


 Calright Instruments explains that an inclined manometer can stretch 12 inches of scale length to represent 1 inch of vertical height. That gives fine resolution for draft, duct and clean room pressures that a vertical tube cannot read well.


 The same differential idea appears in a differential pressure gauge and a differential pressure transmitter , which replaced liquid columns in most plant service.


 Second Worked Example: Inclined Tube


 An inclined manometer uses red oil of density 827 kg per cubic metre at 10 degrees, and the liquid moves 120 mm along the tube. The vertical height is 120 × sin 10° = 120 × 0.1736 = 20.84 mm.


 The pressure is ΔP = 827 × 9.81 × 0.02084 = 169.1 Pa, ignoring the air term. The same 169 Pa would raise a vertical water column by only about 17 mm, so the inclined U tube manometer gives about seven times more scale.


 Choosing the Manometer Fluid


 
 
 Fluid Specific Gravity Typical Use 

 Water with dye 1.00 Draft, duct and low gas pressures 

 Red oil About 0.827 Inclined gauges, finer scale 

 Unity oil 1.00 Stable oil that reads like water 

 Mercury About 13.54 Higher pressures, vacuum, legacy labs 

 



 Thomasnet lists red oil at a specific gravity of 0.827 at 60 °F and high purity mercury at 13.54 at 71.6 °F. Learn how this ratio is defined in what is specific gravity .
